claims.text: Equiatomic FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt alloys produced by conventional casting and annealing are single-phase FCC alloys with low coercivity.
High-energy ball milling followed by rapid consolidation can retain an ultrafine-grained, high-dislocation-density microstructure in an equiatomic FeCoNi-based alloy.
The proposed processing route will produce grain sizes on the order of tens of nanometers.
The ultrafine-grained processed alloy will contain more grain boundaries and defects than a conventionally cast and annealed baseline.
Grain boundaries and dislocation networks in the processed alloy will act as magnetic-domain-wall pinning sites.
Domain-wall pinning increases the energy barriers for reversible domain-wall movement.
Hindered domain-wall motion will increase coercivity relative to a coarse-grained, relatively defect-free conventionally processed alloy.
Ball milling followed by rapid consolidation will increase the coercivity of an equiatomic FeCoNi-based alloy relative to conventionally cast or annealed FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt.
The processed alloy will largely retain the baseline's high saturation magnetization.
The coercivity enhancement will be most pronounced when a grain size of tens of nanometers and a high defect density are retained.
Excessively high post-deformation annealing temperatures can suppress the predicted coercivity enhancement.
Insufficient grain refinement can prevent the predicted coercivity enhancement.
Processing-induced imperfections may reduce saturation magnetization.
Milling at room temperature and consolidation at 700–900 °C under a protective atmosphere should avoid oxidation while retaining the desired microstructure.
